newsitem.title: UAE: Abu Dhabi firm to award $1.2 billion satellite deal.
newsitem.headline: Abu Dhabi firm to award $1.2 billion satellite deal.

text.p: A new Abu Dhabi-based communications firm said Monday it planned to announce within a month the winner of a $1.2 billion deal for a satellite system to extend mobile telecommunications throughout the Arab world.

Thuraya Satellite Telecommunications Co. Chairman Mohammad Hassan Omran told a news conference the company had received final bids from three international firms to design, construct and launch a satellite system by the year 2000 to mainly cover Arab states and the Indian subcontinent.
In the race to supply Thuraya, which in Arabic means the Pleiades or Taurus star cluster, are U.S. firms Hughes and Lockheed Martin and France's Aerospatiale .
"We estimate that over 12 years the cost of the project will be $1.2 billion," Thuraya Project Manager Yousuf al-Sayed said.

Omran said the offers were being scrutinised by Thuraya's executive committee. "(It) will present its recommendations to a meeting of the board of directors on Aug. 26 for selecting the suitable system supplier," he added.
The board would then announce the preferred bidder, Sayed said, to go into the last round of negotiations with Thuraya.
"These should finish by Sept. 9 and on Sept. 10 the board will authorise the chairman to ink the deal, with the signing due to take place on Sept. 11," Sayed said.

Thuraya plans to provide mobile communication services based on a satellite system launched into orbit over the Indian Ocean. It will extend the reach of mobile phones in Arab countries, Iran, Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Central Asia, Turkey and parts of Europe, making services available to remote sea and rural areas.
The first satellite was conservatively forecast to have capacity to handle 1.75 million subscribers, a total expected to be reached within four or five years.
"The less-conservative forecast is 2.4 million subscribers on a single satellite. We can also add another 40 percent capacity with a second satellite," Sayed said.
Chairman Omran said 10 companies had so far committed to taking stakes totalling more than 75 percent in Thuraya, which will be capitalised at $500 million.
